title: Russian help would make North Korea’s missile-test flurry worse news | The Strategist
paragraphs: One of the biggest concerns is that Russia may have helped. North Korea has conducted a flurry of missile tests in the past few weeks. Advances in North Korean missile technology are unwelcome in themselves, but any Russian technical backing behind the effort would indicate a tightening of the Moscow-Pyongyang partnership – and greater potential for more North Korean advances.

There have been at least four sets of North Korean missile launches in the past few weeks. On 20 September, North Korea tested a new missile, thought to be one with a hypersonic warhead. According to a South Korean report, North Korea’s Korea Central News Agency (KCNA) provided no details of the missile tested, but wording on the photo caption released by the agency referred to the ‘Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory’. So it is likely to be an ‘upgraded version of the Hwasong-11MA’ hypersonic missile that North Korea first showcased in 2025. South Korean security analysts believe the Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 ‘combines a KN-23, or Hwasong-11Ga, missile body with a hypersonic glide vehicle-type terminal section’. They describe it as ‘a long-range precision-strike weapon designed to penetrate missile defences through manoeuvrability while striking targets several hundred kilometres away.’

Two weeks later, on 3 October, North Korea fired an intermediate-range missile into the Sea of Japan. According to the Asia-Pacific Security Magazine, the KCNA characterised it as another hypersonic missile test. The KCNA reportedly claimed that the missile had struck a target 1,000 km away, though both South Korea and Japan suggested a smaller range. The North Korean leader’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, also claimed that the missile could ‘manoeuvre at low altitude and incorporated unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities intended to complicate interception.’ Manoeuvring is a characteristic of a hypersonic missile. Kim Yo Jong also asserted the inability of Japan and South Korea to arrive at an accurate picture of the flight details, saying that ‘whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points.’ More worryingly, she also described the missile as ‘strategic’, implying it was designed to deliver nuclear warheads.
